q: In the Jura and the northern Rhone, bunches are dried on mats or hung in ventilated lofts before a very slow winter pressing. What is the wine called?
exp: Paille is straw, and the mats gave the style its name even where the fruit now hangs in crates. Vin jaune is dry and aged under a film of yeast, and macvin is grape juice fortified before it ever ferments.

q: Sun-dried Xynisteri and Mavro from a group of hill villages make a wine Cyprus has been exporting since the crusades. Which wine?
exp: The name comes from the Grande Commanderie, the Knights Hospitaller estate that organised the trade. The grapes are laid out in the sun after picking and the wine is then aged oxidatively.

q: Assyrtiko is left in the sun for a fortnight after picking to make a sweet, tarry, deep amber wine. Which Greek island?
exp: Vinsanto from Santorini is a separate thing from Tuscan Vin Santo, and the shared name has several competing explanations. Assyrtiko keeps ferocious acidity even at three hundred grams of sugar.

q: Berries left hanging on the vine simply shrivel in dry autumn air, with no fungus involved at all. What is that called in French?
exp: Passerillage concentrates sugar exactly as noble rot does, but the flavours stay purer and more apricot-like without the honeyed, savoury layer the fungus adds. Pourriture noble is the French name for noble rot itself.

q: A Cape wine made from Muscat raisined on the vine was among the most prized bottles in Europe two centuries ago. Which wine?
exp: Muscat Blanc a Petits Grains grown below the mountains behind Cape Town, unfortified, and revived in the 1980s after a century out of production. Jane Austen, Dickens and Napoleon's household all have a place in its story.

q: Grapes are laid out on mats in the Andalusian sun until they are close to raisins, then pressed for an almost black, treacly wine. Which variety?
exp: The sun-drying is called the soleo, and it lifts the must to sugar levels no yeast could ever work through. The wine is fortified early and can pour like oil at over four hundred grams of sugar per litre.

q: Terraced schist tumbles almost into the Mediterranean at the Spanish frontier, and the Grenache grown on those slopes makes a sweet red whose fermentation is cut short with spirit. Which appellation?
exp: Four communes of the Cote Vermeille work terraces too steep for any machine, laced with stone channels that carry the storm water off. Maury lies inland in the Agly valley and Rivesaltes on the plain behind Perpignan, while the dry red off these same slopes is sold as Collioure.

q: The addition of spirit to stop a fermentation has a name of its own in French cellars. What is it?
exp: Mutage is the act, and the wine is then said to be muted. Remuage is riddling, soutirage is racking and collage is fining, all quite separate operations.

q: Fresh juice from the Charentes is never allowed to ferment at all: young Cognac goes into it straight away, and the blend then rests in cask before bottling at around seventeen per cent. Which wine is that?
exp: Spirit added before the yeast ever starts makes a vin de liqueur, or mistelle, and its sweetness is simply juice that was never fermented. The other three are built the same way in their own regions, each on a local spirit: Armagnac in Gascony, marc in the Jura, and mostly wine spirit in Champagne.

q: Some Roussillon fortified wines are deliberately left in glass demijohns out of doors, through summer heat and winter cold. What does that develop?
opts: A rancio character of walnut, coffee and dried fig
A veil of yeast giving almond and fresh dough notes
exp: Heat and oxygen together take the wine somewhere no cool reductive cellar could. Rancio is prized rather than avoided here, and the same word describes the character of very old Australian fortifieds.

q: In a hot corner of north-east Victoria, Muscat raisins on the vine, is muted with spirit, then ages for decades in old barrels under tin roofs. Which region?
exp: Summer heat in the sheds drives both concentration and oxidation, and a blending system on solera lines keeps very old material in every bottle. The grape is the red-berried form of Muscat Blanc a Petits Grains, known locally as Brown Muscat.

q: Four tiers of rising age and richness are used for Rutherglen Muscat. Which sits at the top?
exp: Rutherglen Muscat, then Classic, then Grand, then Rare, each a step up in concentration. The ladder is set and policed by the local producers rather than by wine law, with each tier carrying its own band of average age, from three to five years at the base to twenty years or more for Rare.

q: Poached prawns with lemon open the meal and a slow-braised beef shin follows it. Which pair of pours matches each course for weight?
opts: The same sweet fortified wine with both courses
A full-bodied oaked red with the prawns, a light unoaked white with the beef
A light unoaked white with the prawns, a full-bodied red with the beef
The same young tannic red with both courses
exp: Weight is the crudest measure of a dish and the one worth settling before anything is argued about flavour: the prawns vanish under anything heavy and the braise makes a delicate white taste of water. Get the volume right and a mediocre flavour match still drinks well, while getting it wrong cannot be rescued by cleverness later.

q: A fifteen percent oaked red is poured beside a plate of steamed sole. What is the guest most likely to notice?
opts: Both taste much as they did on their own
The fish tastes of almost nothing
The fish tastes markedly saltier than before
The wine tastes thin and sour, its fruit stripped out
exp: An overpowering wine does not improve a delicate dish, it erases it, and the guest usually blames the kitchen rather than the pour. Thin and sour is what happens in the opposite mismatch, when a light white is sent out against a braise.

q: Raw fish dressed with lime, ginger and coriander is feather-light on the plate and very loud in flavour. What does that combination ask of the wine?
opts: Pronounced aroma and flavour carried at a light body
A heavy, high-alcohol wine to match the volume
Firm tannin and a long spell in new oak
Enough sweetness to coat the palate
exp: Weight and intensity are separate axes, and a dish can be extreme on one while modest on the other. An aromatic white at twelve percent carries plenty of flavour without the mass that would flatten raw fish, which is exactly the combination this plate is asking for.

q: A cod fillet arrives blanketed in a butter and cream sauce. Which white is the sounder call?
opts: A white with body and a ripe, rounded texture
A thin, neutral white at eleven percent, served very cold
exp: Cream and butter add weight the fish alone does not have, so a wine that suited the plain poached version now tastes watery beside it. Sweetness is the wrong axis entirely here, and a loudly aromatic wine argues with the sauce instead of supporting it.
